title: Pompeo Invoked an Emergency for $8.1 Billion in Arms Transfers to Three Countries
description_short: On May 24, 2019, Secretary of State Mike Pompeo invoked an emergency to expedite 22 arms transfers worth about $8.1 billion to Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Jordan.
description_medium: Secretary of State Mike Pompeo announced on May 24, 2019, that he had made an emergency determination under Section 36 of the Arms Export Control Act and directed immediate formal notification of 22 pending arms transfers totaling about $8.1 billion to Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Jordan. He cited deterring Iran and building partner self-defense capacity. The action bypassed the ordinary congressional review period.
description_long: On May 24, 2019, Secretary of State Mike Pompeo announced an emergency determination under Section 36 of the Arms Export Control Act and directed the State Department to complete immediate formal notification of 22 pending arms transfers to Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates and Jordan. Pompeo put their combined value at approximately $8.1 billion and said the transfers were intended to deter Iranian aggression and strengthen partner self-defense. A contemporaneous CNN report explained that invoking the emergency allowed the administration to expedite the sales without the ordinary congressional review period. The event was broader than the original title’s two named recipients: Jordan was also included. These sources establish the procedural action, approximate total and stated rationale. They do not provide in the cited press statement a full transfer-by-transfer list of weapons and services, or document the outcome of every congressional response. The revised text states the three recipients and attributes the rationale to the administration without treating it as independently proven or implying every transfer was delivered.

He said the Dayton shooting killed nine people and injured 27, expressed sympathy for victims and survivors, said he had spoken with Ohio Governor Mike DeWine and Dayton Mayor Nan Whaley, and directed federal authorities to provide needed assistance.
prior_proposal.description_long: President Donald Trump delivered remarks on August 5, 2019, in the White House Diplomatic Reception Room about the weekend attacks in Dayton, Ohio, and El Paso, Texas. The official transcript records that he described the Dayton gunman as having killed nine people and injured 27. Trump expressed sympathy for victims, families, and survivors. He said he had spoken with Ohio Governor Mike DeWine and Dayton Mayor Nan Whaley to express support, and that he was in close contact with Attorney General William Barr and FBI Director Christopher Wray. He also said he had directed federal authorities to provide whatever assistance was needed. This proposal describes Trump’s public response as a separate dated statement event; it does not treat him as responsible for the shooting or claim anything about the gunman’s motive. The transcript is the basis for the date, setting, casualty figures as Trump stated them, named contacts, and assistance directive. Keep this separate from any entry about the August 4 attack itself, and deduplicate statement records by the August 5 transcript rather than conflating them with reporting on the attack.

prior_hold: The coordinator and prior proposal leave the shooting entry held because the supplied attack reporting did not itself establish a Trump connection. The official government transcript independently verifies Trump’s direct response on August 5, 2019, so the record can be narrowed to that statement.
The casualty figures in this proposal are explicitly attributed to Trump’s remarks. No independent count or claim about the shooter’s motive is added.
The proposal treats the remarks as a distinct statement event and must remain separate from records describing the August 4 shooting itself.

title: ICE Official Testified That Team Reviewed Student Protester Leads
description_short: An ICE official testified that a 2025 team reviewed student-protester leads, including names from a Canary Mission list, and compiled more than 100 reports.
description_medium: During the Trump administration, ICE official Peter Hatch testified in July 2025 about a specialized team assembled to investigate student-protester leads. The Knight First Amendment Institute’s trial update says Hatch described a Canary Mission list of roughly 5,000 names and more than 100 reports. Related reporting says the team used other sources and sent reports to the State Department for possible action. The testimony does not establish that every person was investigated or targeted for removal.
description_long: During the Trump administration, ICE Homeland Security Investigations official Peter Hatch testified in July 2025 about a specialized “Tiger Team” assembled to investigate student-protester leads. The Knight First Amendment Institute’s contemporaneous trial update says Hatch described a list of roughly 5,000 people identified on Canary Mission and more than 100 resulting reports. Other reporting on the testimony says the team used leads from multiple sources, including Betar, and submitted reports to the State Department for possible action. This is an attributed account of testimony about an investigative process. It does not establish that the online list was an official government blacklist, that every person on it was investigated in the same way, or that every subject faced removal or another enforcement action. The record supports the reported team, list and report counts, with the testimony and agency referrals described as reported; it does not support a claim of a 100–200 report range or blanket targeting of all listed people.

supports: Trial update reports Hatch’s testimony about the Tiger Team, roughly 5,000 Canary Mission names and more than 100 reports.
The July 2025 report places the testimony during the Trump administration.
Reports that leads came from multiple sources and reports were referred to the State Department for possible action.
Contemporaneous reporting on Hatch’s testimony and the investigation process.

rationale: The Knight update and corroborating coverage support a Trump-administration agency investigation described in testimony. The prior title’s use of “anti-war” and its unqualified statement that ICE used a blacklist overstate the evidence; the replacement attributes the process to Hatch’s testimony and identifies the documented scale.

prior_proposal.title: NDSU Report Estimates $14.9 Billion Annualized China Tariff Shortfall
prior_proposal.description_short: A May 2026 NDSU report estimates China’s 2025/26 retaliatory tariffs cut U.S. agricultural exports by $14.9 billion annualized.
prior_proposal.description_medium: A May 2026 North Dakota State University report estimates that China’s retaliatory tariffs reduced U.S. agricultural exports to China by $14.9 billion on an annualized basis during March 2025–February 2026. The model assigns about $6.8 billion of the shortfall to soybeans. These are estimates of China-bound exports and a modeled tariff effect, not measured net losses to farmers or a 72% soybean-export collapse.
prior_proposal.description_long: A May 2026 report by North Dakota State University researchers assessed the effects of China’s 2025/26 retaliatory tariffs on U.S. agricultural exports. Using a structural gravity model, the authors estimated an annualized $14.9 billion shortfall in U.S. exports to China over March 2025 through February 2026, relative to a 2024 export baseline. The report attributes the modeled shortfall to China’s Fentanyl and Reciprocal tariff layers and estimates that soybeans account for about $6.8 billion. It also explains that the model separates tariff effects from other influences, including global commodity trends, exporter and importer shocks, seasonality, and monthly aggregate shocks. The figure is an estimate of China-bound export sales, not a direct measure of net harm to U.S. farmers. The report does not support the source record’s claim of a 72% soybean-export collapse. The AgEcon Search record dates the report to May 19, 2026, so this proposal treats the item as report-publication context and corrects the March 4, 2025 record date rather than presenting the later estimate as known on that date.

prior_hold: The official NDSU report and its repository metadata support a May 2026 report-publication item with a model-estimated $14.9B annualized China-bound export shortfall over March 2025–February 2026, including a $6.8B soybean estimate. This is not the source record’s March 4, 2025 event and does not support its 72% soybean claim; draft is publication context only and explicitly corrects the record date if adopted. Within the assigned four-key subset, no duplicate report event was identified.

title: Prosecutor Email Said Trump Flew on Epstein’s Jet at Least Eight Times, 1993–1996
description_short: Reuters reported that a prosecutor’s email said flight records listed Trump on at least eight Epstein-jet flights from 1993 to 1996.
description_medium: Reuters reported in December 2025 that a January 2020 email from an unidentified New York prosecutor said flight records listed Donald Trump as a passenger on at least eight Epstein-jet flights between 1993 and 1996. The email said Ghislaine Maxwell was aboard at least four. This attributes the count to the email; the report does not itself allege wrongdoing by Trump.
description_long: Reuters reported on December 23, 2025, that newly released Epstein-related records included a January 2020 email from an unidentified New York prosecutor discussing flight records. According to Reuters, the email said Donald Trump was listed as a passenger on at least eight flights on Jeffrey Epstein’s private jet between 1993 and 1996, including at least four flights on which Ghislaine Maxwell was also listed. The report also described other passengers named in the email. The supported claim is that the prosecutor’s email summarized flight records with that count and date range; this account attributes the details to Reuters’ reporting of the email. The packet does not independently recount the underlying logs, and the passenger listing by itself does not establish participation in or knowledge of Epstein’s crimes. The earlier count of 11 flights and date range through 1998 are not supported by the cited report. Claims about recruitment or other conduct are outside this documented flight-record account.

supports: Reuters reports that a January 2020 prosecutor email said records listed Trump on at least eight Epstein-jet flights between 1993 and 1996, at least four with Ghislaine Maxwell.
Reuters describes the released records and other passengers; the listing alone does not establish criminal conduct.

rationale: The pinned Reuters fact mapping supports the flight count and date range as statements in a prosecutor email. The correction removes the unsupported count of 11 and unrelated recruitment claims and does not infer wrongdoing from passenger listings.

title: Wisconsin GOP Said It Trained More Than 5,000 Election Observers for 2024
description_short: Reuters reported that the RNC and Wisconsin Republican Party said they trained more than 5,000 election observers in Wisconsin.
description_medium: Reuters reported on October 31, 2024, that the Republican National Committee and Republican Party of Wisconsin said they had trained more than 5,000 election observers in the state. The report also described separate grassroots groups planning to deploy observers and monitor ballot drop boxes. It does not establish that Trump personally directed the training or that the program was a statewide voter-intimidation operation.
description_long: In an October 31, 2024 report about election observers in Wisconsin, Reuters said the Republican National Committee and Republican Party of Wisconsin reported training more than 5,000 observers. The article separately described grassroots groups that planned to deploy up to 1,500 observers collectively at voting sites and count centers and to monitor ballot drop boxes. It also reported local election officials’ concerns about observer conduct during earlier absentee-ballot processing in Milwaukee-area communities. Those facts support reporting on party training and local organizing, with attribution to the groups and officials. They do not show that Donald Trump personally deployed the observers, establish a nationwide strategy, or prove that all observers engaged in intimidation. The original headline combined separate actors and allegations into one claim that the source does not establish. This account focuses on the verifiable training statement and attributes separate deployment plans without treating them as completed activity.

supports: Reuters reports the RNC and Wisconsin Republican Party said they trained more than 5,000 observers.
Reuters separately describes grassroots groups’ plans, and local officials’ concerns about earlier observer conduct.

rationale: The cited Reuters report supports the training statement and separately attributes grassroots deployment plans and officials’ concerns. The copy distinguishes plans from actions and removes unsupported personal direction by Trump and blanket intimidation claims.

title: Foreign Government Payments to Trump Businesses Prompted Emoluments Lawsuits
description_short: Court filings and a congressional report documented foreign-government-linked spending at Trump properties and emoluments allegations.
description_medium: An amended complaint in the D.C. and Maryland case cited Saudi-agent disclosures reporting payments to Trump’s Washington hotel. A House Oversight report, issued by Democratic committee members and based on a limited set of Mazars records, identified at least $7.8 million in payments from 20 foreign governments to Trump businesses during his presidency. The plaintiffs alleged violations of the Foreign Emoluments Clause; the records establish payments and allegations, not a court finding of unconstitutionality.
description_long: An amended complaint filed by the attorneys general of the District of Columbia and Maryland cited foreign-agent disclosures reporting payments by an agent for Saudi Arabia to the Trump International Hotel in Washington. It listed $190,272 for lodging, $78,204 for catering and $1,568 for parking during a six-month period spanning October 2016 through March 2017, and alleged that some payments came after Trump’s inauguration. Separately, a House Oversight report based on Mazars accounting records identified at least $7.8 million in payments from 20 foreign governments to Trump businesses during his presidency. The report was issued by Democratic committee members and described a limited portion of records. The D.C. and Maryland plaintiffs argued that foreign-government-linked payments violated the Foreign Emoluments Clause. The complaint records allegations and the House report describes payments in its reviewed records; neither, on its own, establishes a final constitutional merits ruling. These sources support an attributed account of spending and litigation, not a categorical claim that the Constitution was violated.

supports: The amended complaint cites FARA disclosures for Saudi-agent payments to the Washington hotel, including lodging, catering and parking amounts.

title: Colorado Lawsuit Cites White House Email on Federal Actions Toward the State
description_short: Colorado attorneys cited a December 2025 White House email inviting agencies to discuss immediate actions concerning the state.
description_medium: CBS Colorado reported that Colorado attorneys cited a December 15, 2025 email from White House staffer Emily Underwood in a lawsuit alleging retaliation over election policy and the prosecution of Tina Peters. The message invited officials from several agencies to discuss “immediate actions” concerning Colorado. The White House disputed a connection to Peters, so the email is evidence cited by plaintiffs, not a judicial finding of retaliation.
description_long: News reports describe a December 15, 2025 email from White House staffer Emily Underwood inviting officials at five federal agencies to discuss “immediate actions” concerning Colorado. The message reportedly said the goal was to prioritize the state so grants and federal support aligned with administration priorities. Colorado attorneys cited the email in a lawsuit alleging retaliation tied to the state’s election policy and the prosecution of Tina Peters. Reporting says the email’s contents were read aloud at a court hearing and that the message itself did not mention Peters. The White House disputed that the discussion was tied to Peters and said it concerned multiple policy issues. The email and the parties’ positions are described in news coverage of ongoing litigation; the state’s retaliation theory remains an allegation, not a final judicial finding. This account concerns the email and how the parties characterize it. It does not claim that Trump personally directed unlawful retaliation or rely on an uncited legal assertion about the limits of presidential clemency.

supports: Email date and sender, agency invitees, how Colorado attorneys presented it in litigation, and the White House’s denial of a connection to Tina Peters.
Court-transcript reporting on the email and the state’s retaliation allegation.
Email timing, sender, recipients, quoted language, and the state’s retaliation lawsuit.
Republished New York Times report on the email, its stated purpose, hearing disclosure, and that it did not mention Peters.

rationale: The cited reports support the email and the competing positions in litigation. The correction removes the unsupported clemency-authority clause and keeps retaliation attributed to the plaintiffs rather than presented as a finding.
